title: Meaningful Human Deviation Pattern
description: A pattern for ensuring a human reviewer positioned 'in the loop' of an automated scoring system genuinely can and does deviate from the score, measured by an observable deviation rate, rather than the review being a symbolic formality that leaves the score de facto controlling.
problem: A human reviewer nominally positioned between an automated score and a final decision can still leave the score in full control if the reviewer lacks the authority, time, or information to meaningfully disagree — making the 'human in the loop' safeguard illusory while still technically satisfying a policy requirement for human review.
solution: Give the human reviewer genuine authority and sufficient context to deviate from the score, and measure the deviation rate as an ongoing metric: a rate at or near zero is itself evidence the review is symbolic rather than meaningful, and should trigger a redesign of the review process.
applicability: Any process where a human formally reviews or approves an automated system's score or recommendation before it takes effect on an individual.
consequences: A deviation-rate metric can be gamed by encouraging token deviations that don't reflect genuine reconsideration; giving reviewers more authority to deviate can reduce consistency across cases if not paired with clear criteria for when deviation is appropriate.

citations.title: Judgment of the Court (First Chamber), 7 December 2023 — OQ v Land Hessen (SCHUFA Holding, Scoring), Case C-634/21
citations.publisher: Court of Justice of the European Union

relationships.reason: A measured, genuine deviation rate is the concrete mechanism satisfying this control's human-intervention safeguard.
The pattern's output is an observable human deviation rate log.
